newsitem.title: UK: Study links two human "mad cow" diseases.
newsitem.headline: Study links two human "mad cow" diseases.

text.p: British experts in brain disease said on Friday they had found evidence linking two human versions of mad cow disease.

They said they found similarities in the brains of patients who had died of a new strain of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) and two who died of kuru, a similar brain illness that used to kill off cannibals in Papua New Guinea.
John Collinge of the Neurogenetics Unit at St Mary's Hospital in London and other scientists said they were checking the assumption that such brain diseases were related when they found the evidence.

Scientists fear a new variant of CJD, a deadly and brain-wasting illness, was caused by people eating beef products from cattle infected with bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease).

It is also assumed that the New Guinea cannibals got kuru from their habit of eating the bodies of deceased loved ones -- brains and all. But no one had compared brain samples of the two groups of victims.
Collinge's group did so and found many similarities in the distinctive areas of abnormal prion proteins associated with such diseases.
"This preliminary study shows that there are similarities between the new variant CJD and kuru, particularly in the pattern of prion deposition," they wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.
This could reflect a common route for infection by both CJD and kuru -- that is, eating infected material.

They also noted that CJD can occur sporadically -- one in a million people get it every year for unknown reasons. Although it is assumed a genetic mutation is responsible, it could be some cases are due to some kind of exposure to abnormal prions, they said.
Working with another group, Collinge found that dairy farmers who came down with CJD did not have the new variant.
"Before the recognition of the new variant of CJD, concern was raised at the greater-than-expected occurrence of CJD in UK dairy farmers," they wrote in a second Lancet letter.
However, examination of their brains showed they did not die of the new variant, they said.
Other scientists reported this week they are closing in on the mysterious infectious agent involved in BSE and CJD.
Michael Ter-Avanesyan and colleagues at the Institute of Experimental Cardiology in Moscow said they were able to get yeast to act like the abnormal prion proteins.

Prions, normal brain proteins, take on an abnormal, folded shape in BSE, CJD and their cousins. Some scientists think an unknown agent or a "slow virus" is responsible, while most say abnormal prions somehow infect normal ones.
Ter-Avanesyan's group studied a yeast protein Sup35p, which exists in both a normal and folded form like prions.
Reporting in the journal Science, they said exposure of the normal protein to abnormal protein was enough to convert it.
James Hope and colleagues at Britain's Institute for Animal Health said on Wednesday they had made similar findings. They purified BSE and CJD prions and exposed them to normal human prions.
